subject: Agriculture
title: China's Great Famine
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: China's Great Famine.

hook.text: Between 1959 and 1961, up to 45 million Chinese people starved. It was the deadliest famine in history.

buildup.text: Mao's Great Leap Forward collectivized farms and imposed disastrous agricultural policies.

discovery.text: Officials falsified harvest reports to meet quotas. The government exported grain while millions died.

twist.text: Farmers were forced to melt tools for steel instead of harvesting. Crops rotted in fields.

climax.text: After the famine, China reversed course—eventually adopting Green Revolution seeds and market reforms.

punchline.text: Bad policy can starve a nation faster than bad weather.

quiz.question: What government policy caused China's Great Famine?
options: Mao's Great Leap Forward forced collectivization and disastrous farming mandates

details.summary: China's Great Famine of 1959-1961 killed an estimated 15-55 million people, making it the deadliest famine in human history. It was primarily caused by the disastrous agricultural policies of the Great Leap Forward, combined with drought and political repression of accurate reporting.
details.whyItMatters: The Great Famine demonstrated how catastrophically wrong centrally planned agriculture can go. It ultimately led to China's agricultural reforms in the 1980s and its embrace of hybrid rice technology that made China food self-sufficient.
takeaways: China's Great Famine killed an estimated 15-55 million people from 1959 to 1961
Mao's Great Leap Forward forced collectivization and pseudoscientific farming methods
The disaster eventually led to China's agricultural reforms and embrace of hybrid rice

faq.question: What agricultural policies caused China's Great Famine?
faq.answer: The Great Leap Forward forced farmers into communes, banned private farming, and mandated pseudoscientific planting methods like deep plowing and close spacing. Local officials inflated harvest reports to meet quotas, causing the government to export food while millions starved internally.

faq.question: How did the Great Famine shape China's later agricultural policy?
faq.answer: After the famine, China gradually abandoned collective farming. The 1978 household responsibility system returned land to families. China heavily invested in hybrid rice research led by Yuan Longping, whose varieties eventually doubled rice yields and made China largely food self-sufficient.
